You never change a live domain directly. You work in a private copy, check
it, and switch it live in one step when it is ready. That copy is a
**draft**, and the switch is **publish**. This page shows the lifecycle, what
a draft allows, and what publish verifies before it commits.

## The lifecycle

Two doors open a draft. **New domain** starts from an empty one. **Edit
existing** forks a live domain — the structure comes over, the data does
not. Either way the draft gets an autogenerated name that starts with `_`,
so it can never collide with a live name. You set the publish target name
yourself, in the draft's **Name** field.

Inside a draft, Facet lifts the version rules that protect live data:

- the schema version may decrease or skip ahead,
- a field can be removed or change its type at the same version,
- a version bump needs no migration function,
- everything else still validates: field names, action names, script
  compilation.

The live domain keeps serving its current definitions while you edit. Your
changes reach other users only when you publish.

## What publish checks

Publish is one transaction, and it re-validates everything that involves the
target. Before it writes anything, it verifies that:

- the target name uses lowercase letters, digits and dashes, and starts with
  a letter. A leading `_` answers `422` — that prefix is reserved for drafts,
- the source is a draft, read under a row lock,
- the composition graph is closed: every `children:` entry has a matching
  `member_of` on the child, and back,
- in fresh mode (the default), the target name is free. A name a live domain
  already holds answers `409`,
- in overwrite mode (`overwrite: true`), every doctype whose structure
  differs from the live one carries a `schema_version` of exactly the live
  version plus one, with a migration function for that step. A doctype whose
  structure is identical publishes as it is.

The publish dialog shows these results — the issue counts, the version gate,
the grant tickets — before you confirm.

## Why test documents never reach production

Publish copies the structure only: the doctype definitions, their view
templates, and the domain document. The documents you created while testing
are scratch. Without an extra choice, they are soft-deleted with the draft,
and nothing you typed while experimenting ends up in production data.

You can carry chosen scratch documents over: the publish dialog has an
**Import existing documents** option, and the API takes a `documents` field
on `POST /Api/core/Domain/:id/publish`. It imports per doctype, and only
into a target that does not define that doctype yet — a selection that
collides with existing production rows answers `422`, so draft rows never
merge into production rows.

## How it works

This section is for the reader who wants the full mechanism.

**The flag, not the prefix.** A draft is a real `core.Domain` document with
a `draft: true` flag. Every guard keys off the flag; the `_` prefix is
cosmetic. The name is autogenerated (a `_` plus a unique suffix), so users
never pick a draft name.

**Copy-and-drop, not a rename.** Publish copies each doctype definition and
its view templates into the target, relinks the same-domain reference
targets to the new name, carries the draft's co-editors over, and then drops
the draft. The mutation log is append-only, so a rename in place would
rewrite history; copy-and-drop gives the target fresh rows under its own
identity. A crash before commit rolls back to an intact draft — retry the
same publish.

**Overwrite mode preserves the live domain document.** The target keeps its
description, its context sets, and its hooks. A hook declared in the draft
but missing on the live domain comes back as a warning on the publish
response — the workaround is to edit the live domain's hooks. The live view
templates converge to the draft's: changed ones update, draft-only ones are
created, live-only ones are deleted. Saved collection views are never
touched.

**Replication stays inert in a draft.** A draft is excluded as a replication
source and as a consumer, so a `replicate` field cannot be exercised before
publish. You can declare it — it is schema-valid — and the first publish
over the target runs the full replication validation. This is the one
definition surface that does not fire in draft mode.

**One draft per live domain.** Forking a domain that already has an open
draft answers `409`. Discard or publish the first draft before you fork
again.

**A forked draft does not track its source.** The live domain and the draft
drift apart independently, and the gate compares them only at publish.

**A stale cache of one or two seconds.** A saved definition reaches the
running server through an event. A document write that lands within about
one to two seconds of the save can still run the old definition — re-test
after a short wait before you judge a fix.

**A live doctype the draft no longer defines stays on the target.** Publish
only touches doctypes the draft defines. Deleting a doctype that holds live
data has its own semantics and is out of scope for the publish action.

:::tip
Run **Check** before you publish. It reports the per-doctype issues — broken
references, template problems, missing views — and the publish confirmation
shows the same list. See [Check before you publish](/build/model/in-app/check-before-publish/).
:::
